column6: Two snapshot defects. tarHeader() splits a path longer than 100 bytes at an arbitrary byte offset instead of at a ustar slash, so tools/ plus 110 a-chars plus .mjs restores as tools/aaaaaaaaaaaaaa/…mjs: the payload hash can be right and the path still wrong. And collectSourcePaths accepts a symlink and statSync follows it, while the exclusion policy only inspects the link's own name, so an alias in the manifest can point at a .env-shaped target and the snapshot copies it.
column7: tests/regression/source-identity.test.mjs "a path longer than the name field is split at a separator, not at a byte offset", "a snapshot restores the paths, modes and bytes the manifest names" and "a symlink is recorded as a link, and never read through". The round-trip reader in the test is written from the ustar layout rather than from the writer, and the same paths are also listed by the system tar, so a writer that agrees only with itself cannot pass.
column8: tools/frontend-source-identity.mjs: splitUstarPath() splits name/prefix at a slash byte, taking the first separator that leaves both fields non-empty and inside 100/155 bytes, and refuses a path with no such separator; symlinkTarget() reads a link as a path and never as content and refuses one that leaves the repository; buildManifest() uses lstat and records a link as kind=symlink with its target hashed as a string; buildSnapshot() writes type 2 with the target as the body. A third defect was found while testing: a git mode was being written straight into the ustar mode field, so a regular file's four-digit git mode was restored as an eight-digit octal permission set and a link's type-2 mode as a nonsense one, and the two encodings are now translated explicitly by ustarMode().

column10: The probe copied a fake marker, not a real credential, and there is no evidence that any delivered artefact leaked a secret; this finding reopens the reconstructable-and-safe-snapshot claim of FR9-05 rather than adding to it. A path with no ustar-legal split is refused rather than stored, so a repository containing one cannot be snapshotted at all: PAX would express it, and adding a second on-disk format to keep the output byte-stable was judged a worse trade than an error that names the limit. Symlinks inside the repository are recorded, not refused, and a link reaching an excluded path is flagged targetExcluded rather than dropped, because the link itself is not secret and hiding that one exists would be worse than saying so. One earlier unit run, r9-t5-unit-20260928T092630Z-1, exited 254 because the wrapper was invoked from the repository root rather than from tests/ and npm found no package.json; it is kept in the evidence as history and backs nothing here.

The second says the install key follows the lockfile and names the platform, Node ABI and Playwright version, that an absent install is missing while a stale one is refused, and that a stamp whose node_modules is missing does not pass as current. The last case here is the one that was found by running the old check: a hand-made directory named frontend-browser-run.something-else matched the name pattern and was deleted with its contents.
column8: tools/browser-gate-env.mjs is new and holds the decisions that have to be checked rather than trusted: createScratch mints a per-run directory with a marker file, isOwned and cleanupScratch require that marker, installKey hashes the lockfile with the platform, ABI, Node and Playwright versions and the browsers path, and verifyInstall refuses anything else rather than repairing it. tools/run-browser-gate.sh now allocates through it, cleans up only on an EXIT trap naming the directory it minted, chooses its own two ports, exports the copy's identity digest to the producer, and writes a served.json beside the evidence. tests/browser/fake-api.mjs reports the root it serves and hashes what it returns, and tests/browser/served-source-identity.spec.mjs is in the mock config and compares both against the tree the spec runs from.
column9: r9-t7-browser-20260928T102357Z-1 browser 41/41, exit 0, source digest unchanged before and after, run through the rewritten wrapper rather than the old one. The chain it closes is checkable in three files: reports/evidence/browser-r9-t7-browser-served.json records the source digest, the two ports and the install key the wrapper chose; the run's own .meta records the same digest as source_digest; and the three served-source-identity cases assert at run time that the static server was answering from the tree that digest describes.
column10: One earlier run through the same wrapper, r9-t7-browser-20260928T095049Z-1, exited 1 with 35 passed and 6 failed, and is kept in the evidence: it is what found the egress-policy gap recorded against FR10-08, and it backs nothing here. It is named in this column rather than beside the green count because a cell that quotes a count is leaning on the run it names, and that run did not pass. A provenance gap, not a demonstrated incident: there is no evidence in the R8 review that a browser run ever loaded the wrong source. Hashing the lockfile proves the file is present, not that the installed tree matches it. The served-root check is an assertion in the suite rather than a check the wrapper performs after the fact: a check performed afterwards cannot fail the run it is checking, and a spec that fails is the only version of this that stops a run against the wrong source. Two limits are deliberate and stated here. The ports are chosen by binding port 0, closing it and letting the server take it, so there is a window in which another process could take the port first; a collision surfaces as a Playwright webServer start-up timeout rather than as a run against somebody else's server, because the config sets reuseExistingServer to false. And the static gate runs before the browser suite rather than inside it, so twenty minutes of browser are not spent discovering that the reports do not validate; it is the same npm script, run once, on the same copy. Nothing here has been shown to be exploitable, and the concurrency case was not reproduced against the old wrapper on a reviewer's machine: what is shown is that two runs now receive different directories, that a cleanup refuses any directory it did not create, and that a stale install is refused rather than replaced. The install cache is keyed by lockfile, platform, Node ABI, Node and Playwright versions and the browsers path, and it lives under the user's cache directory, so two runs on one machine share it safely precisely because the key is the content and not a name.

column6: expectBlocked(count) splices entries by count alone, and an undefined count clears the whole list, so a declaration does not pin the URL, method or reason it is claiming. The newContext wrapper also does not require serviceWorkers:block, and the guard uses context.route, whose coverage of Service Worker, redirect and WebSocket traffic is not established.
column7: tests/regression/harness-boundaries.test.mjs "FR10-08: a provoked refusal has to be named, not counted" (7 subtests) and "every context the run creates has service workers blocked" (2 subtests); tests/browser/harness-egress.spec.mjs declares url/method/reason/count at all three provocation sites
column8: tests/browser/helpers/browser-fixture.mjs installEgressGuard guard.expectBlocked (per-declaration matching, both directions fail) and guard.undeclared; withServiceWorkersBlocked applied by both patched methods; tests/browser/fixtures.js context teardown reads undeclared()

column10: Service workers are blocked rather than intercepted, so the policy is proven as an absence of the capability and not as a canary that a registration was refused. No spec in this suite registers one, so a registration path has no runtime evidence either way. Interception of redirects and WebSockets is still unevidenced and stays outside the claim. One gap in the policy itself was found by the first real run through the fixed wrapper, not by reading the code: the shape rule covered gstatic's /s/<family>/v<n>/<file>.woff2, which is what the pinned stylesheet lists, but not /l/font?kit=…&skey=…, which is what Chromium actually asks for when a glyph falls outside the listed unicode ranges. The guard refused twenty-two such requests and failed three tests — intermittently, because whether the request is made at all depends on what the font cache holds, so the same code passed on the next run. A second shape rule now covers that one path, with the sibling paths still refused. That rule originally matched on URL and had no method dimension, which it said rather than implying a restriction it did not enforce; FR11-05 has since given it one. The rule is still open in one respect, and it is not this one: kit remains opaque, because the token is minted per subset by Google and there is nothing in this repository to validate it against. What FR11-05 changed is the rule's own terms, not the reason to keep it. tests/regression/harness-boundaries.test.mjs pins both the allowance and the siblings that must stay refused, and the canary was checked by pointing the static server at the wrong tree: two of the three served-source assertions failed and named both roots.

column6: The four call sites that decide where reports and evidence live each decided for themselves: validate-reports.mjs derived them from repoRoot, the two gate wrappers hardcoded ${REPO_ROOT}/reports/evidence, and the run-claims generator had its own default again. Two of them read no environment at all, so a reader who exported FRONTEND_EVIDENCE_DIR for a package layout watched the tool validate an empty evidence directory and report every claim backed; and the wrappers took a relative --out verbatim, so npm --prefix tests (cwd tests/) resolved it to tests/reports/evidence - a directory the wrapper had just created, so the run passed against evidence it had invented for itself.
column7: tools/frontend-report-paths.mjs is new (5 cases: the precedence and which layer answered, the cwd independence, the absolute path left alone, the evidence default following the reports, the injectable default); tests/regression/report-paths.test.mjs exercises each of the three layers.
column8: tools/frontend-report-paths.mjs holds one resolveReportPaths used by tools/validate-reports.mjs, tools/frontend-run-claims.mjs and both wrappers. Precedence is option, then environment, then default; each path resolves independently and the source layer is returned rather than assumed. Relative paths resolve against the repo root, never against process.cwd(). A relative --out from /tmp now resolves to <repo>/reports/evidence, which is the property that failed.
column9: r10-final-static-20260929T025612Z-1 exit 0 (static gate, whose last step is the validator), and r10-final-unit-20260929T025619Z-1 unit 368/368. The hermetic half is measured rather than asserted: the same 368 tests pass plain, and pass under the gate's own FRONTEND_REPORTS_DIR/FRONTEND_EVIDENCE_DIR, and under a foreign layout only the one case that reports the missing evidence root fails - which is that layout's true state. Before the fixture fix the gate exported those two variables and 35 unrelated cases failed while a plain npm run stayed green.
column10: A resolver can only be as honest as its callers, and four callers were the finding, so the change is a module plus four edits that all had to be made; a fifth consumer added later would reintroduce the disagreement and nothing here would notice. The default evidence directory follows the resolved reports directory, so a reader who moves only FRONTEND_REPORTS_DIR gets evidence beside the reports rather than in the source tree - a decision, and it would be wrong for a reader who wanted them separate, which is why FRONTEND_EVIDENCE_DIR exists. Nothing here has been shown to be exploitable, and no run has been shown to have filed its evidence in the wrong directory; what is shown is that the two ways it could happen are no longer available through the code, and that a gate now prints the directory it chose and the layer that chose it.

column6: validate-reports.mjs compared a source manifest's declared digest against the digest the sidecar claimed and against the .meta, so a manifest whose files list had been edited, or whose count did not match its list, passed as long as the declared numbers agreed with each other. Two declared digests agreeing is a claim about the declaration; nothing recomputed the hash over the bytes.
column7: tests/regression/validate-reports.test.mjs 42 cases; the fixtures were rewritten because the new check rejected them, and each negative case now differs from the baseline in exactly one field.
column8: validate-reports.mjs calls digestOf from tools/frontend-source-identity.mjs and recomputes every source-before and source-after manifest, comparing the result against the recorded digest, checking each entry is a record with a path and a hash, and checking fileCount against the list length. Both declared digests and the count are separate claims and are checked separately, because a manifest can agree with its own digest and still miscount.
column9: r10-final-static-20260929T025612Z-1 exit 0 — đây là static gate, bước cuối của nó là validator — và r10-final-unit-20260929T025619Z-1 unit 368/368. Con số 215 evidence / 49 claim là trạng thái validator *sau* khi matrix và sidecar đã cập nhật, nên nó không thuộc run nào ở trên: nó được kiểm riêng trên một clone sạch (28 rows, 215 evidence, 49 claim bound, exit 0). The check is the production digestOf, so the test and the tool cannot disagree about what a digest is.
column10: The fixture rewrite is the honest part and it is a change to tests rather than to the tool: the fixtures wrote fileCount 1 beside an empty files list with a digest pasted in from the caller, which the new check rejects, and they now build a manifest through digestOf so each case differs from the baseline in one field. That is a stronger baseline than before, not a weaker one. A mismatch reports the list and the digest and the count and does not name which entry was edited, because the digest is one value over the whole list and a guessed filename would send a reader to audit a file nobody touched. Mode is read as a git-mode string (100644), not as a number, because an earlier Number.isInteger check accused every honest manifest of being malformed on every genuine mismatch. What is not shown is that a real producer would have failed: no production manifest in this repository is malformed, and the case is therefore a constructed one, which is the only way to construct it.

column6: tests/browser/fake-api.mjs reported the static root it served and the digest the wrapper had exported, and the spec compared the payload to the environment variable that produced it. A wrapper that copied the wrong tree, a stale FRONTEND_SERVED_DIGEST left in the shell, or another checkout's server already holding the port all produced a run whose claim was internally consistent while the assertions were about a different repository than the reports would name.
column7: tests/regression/served-source-identity.test.mjs is new (4 cases at the HTTP level, including a wrapper claim that is wrong and a run with no claim at all); tests/browser/served-source-identity.spec.mjs gains a fifth browser case.
column8: tests/browser/fake-api.mjs now reports actualStaticDigest, computed once at first use from buildManifest(REPO_ROOT) - the same function the evidence and the validator use, because a second digest routine in the fake API would be a second definition of the source and the two would drift. The spec compares the payload against the tree it is running from, and against the wrapper's claim when there is one.
column9: browser-r10-browser-20260929T025733Z-1 browser 42/42 exit 0, source_drift none, and reports/evidence/browser-r10-browser-served.json records the digest 8679021ddb0c6a694c9a687decf6c86cab191137a41b7b5fb906d1f18f65e452, the two ports and the install key the wrapper chose; the run's own .meta records the same digest as source_digest. The unit-level cases pass the wrong claim through the environment deliberately, so the claim and the tree visibly disagree.
column10: The digest is computed at first probe and cached, so a tree edited during a browser run keeps reporting the digest it started with; that is intended (a run is about one source) and it means the check cannot notice a mid-run edit, which buildSnapshot and the drift check cover instead. The static server root and the spec's root are compared resolved, so the two differ by a trailing separator and by nothing else. The real-app and loopback specs run against a prepared backend, which is still pending, so what is shown is the mock path and the identity of the tree under it.

column6: verifyInstall asked whether node_modules existed. An empty node_modules answers that correctly and is worthless: reproduction with a correct key, the right platform and ABI, node_modules present and empty gave verify-install printing current and exiting 0, then prepare-install returned built:false and handed that tree to the browser run. Every digest in the resulting evidence would have been correct.
column7: tests/regression/browser-gate-isolation.test.mjs 15 cases; the fixture wrote a lockfile with a fake sha and no tree, and now writes a resolved tree. Two cases are new.
column8: tools/browser-gate-env.mjs replaces the existence check with a coverage check against the lockfile the install is stamped for. The lockfile is copied into the cache beside the tree, so the answer needs nothing from the repository and cannot be satisfied by a matching key alone. v2/v3 packages and v1 dependencies are both read; the lockfile's own os and cpu filters are honoured, because npm ci on Linux never installs fsevents and requiring it turned a working install stale on the first run. optional alone does not excuse an absence. prepareInstall refuses a stale install by throwing rather than rebuilding it.
column9: r10-final-unit-20260929T025619Z-1 unit 368/368, and the new case asserts the reproduction end to end: a stamp over an install missing one of the two packages its lockfile declares is stale, names node_modules/beta and 1 of its 2, and prepareInstall throws rather than returning built:false. The mutation of reverting to existsSync is caught.
column10: Two cases assert a missing directory is refused and a directory that is not a directory is refused, which is cheap and kept because the coverage check reads the tree and a file called node_modules would otherwise be counted. Symlinks into the workspace are skipped as link entries, so a lockfile that resolves a dependency by link is not required to have a directory for it - correct for npm, and it means a tree could satisfy the check while the link points somewhere outside it. A real install is still trusted to npm ci to have installed what the lockfile says, so this proves the tree is not obviously incomplete, not that it is byte-identical to a fresh install.

column6: The /l/font shape added by FR10-08 matched on URL and had no method dimension, so a GET and a POST to the same path were the same request as far as the policy was concerned. FR10-08's own limitation recorded that gap and left it open: the rule had to stay because the request is intermittent, but nothing said what it would let through.
column7: tests/regression/harness-boundaries.test.mjs 48 cases; the /l/font case is rewritten because the shape it described no longer exists, and five new refusals are asserted.
column8: tests/browser/helpers/browser-fixture.mjs: GSTATIC_DYNAMIC_FONT_KEYS is {kit, skey, v} and the shape requires exactly one non-empty kit, refuses an unknown key, refuses a repeated key, and carries method GET. createEgressPolicy.reasonFor takes {method} and the guard passes request.method(). A shape-only host is no longer told it is not allowed to be used; it is told what about it failed.
column9: r10-final-unit-20260929T025619Z-1 unit 368/368 with the new refusals asserted, and browser-r10-browser-20260929T025733Z-1 browser 42/42 with no gstatic request refused. The narrowing is derived from the request Chromium is observed to send, and that observation is written down where the rule lives: tools/browser/helpers/browser-fixture.mjs names the two shapes it allows on that origin - a versioned .woff2 under a family the pinned stylesheet lists, and /l/font with kit and skey - rather than allowing a host and hoping. What the rule does not give is proof that it is still needed. FR10-08 recorded this request as intermittent, so a run that never makes it cannot tell a working rule from a dead one, and the fresh 42/42 says nothing either way: it shows the narrowed rule refuses nothing the suite needs, not that the suite needed it.
column10: kit stays opaque and unchecked, and that is stated in the rule rather than implied: the token is minted per subset by Google, so there is nothing in this repository to validate it against, and a non-empty check is a shape, not an authentication. The rule can still break on a legitimate upstream change - a fourth query key, or a repeated one - and that failure would be a refused font and a red test rather than a security problem. Because the endpoint is reached only when a glyph falls outside the pinned unicode ranges, a run whose font cache differs from the observed one may not make the request at all, so a green run is not evidence that the shape is exercised; the unit cases exercise it directly for that reason.

column6: Nothing in the codebase asked how executability is decided, and the three questions it can mean - is it executable, is it 0755, and will a restore put 0755 back - were all answerable with a bitmask. A file restored as 0700 satisfies any bitmask, so mode loss hides behind a correct yes. The extraction side was worse: tar was called without -p, so a restrictive umask genuinely strips the group and other bits from a 0755 entry on restore, and a check that only asked is-it-executable would have reported 0700 as fine.
column7: tests/regression/source-identity.test.mjs 38 cases, of which 9 are new; the umask table is measured rather than asserted and the no--p counterfactual is included.
column8: tools/frontend-source-identity.mjs: hasExecuteBit is the single classifier; MANIFEST_MODES is {100755, 100644}, the only modes Git stores; MODE_CONTRACT states the exact mode a restore must produce per classification; SNAPSHOT_EXTRACT_ARGS is ['-xzpf'] and preservesPermissions derives from the flags whether they carry -p, so the property is testable against flags that do not preserve it. All three inline tar calls route through extractSnapshot, which uses those arguments and nothing else.
column9: r10-final-unit-20260929T025619Z-1 unit 368/368; dropping -p from SNAPSHOT_EXTRACT_ARGS fails 2 cases. The umask measurement is honest about this machine: it runs as root, where the stored mode is restored whatever the umask, so the suite asserts that agreement rather than pretending to the umask-077 difference, and the 0700 outcome - which is what the reviewer's unprivileged run saw - is not reproducible here and is said so.
column10: The 0700 result is therefore carried as a documented measurement from an unprivileged run, not as a live assertion on this machine, and a reader running the suite as an unprivileged user will get the stronger version: atRestrictiveUmask.without === 0o700 and .withP === 0o755. A default-ACL case is not covered at all: setfacl is not available here, and the umask evidence does not speak to default ACLs. hasExecuteBit given a git mode string coerces to a number and returns the right answer for 100755 and 100644 by accident of the decimal digits rather than by design; the contract is a numeric mode and gitMode is the only caller, and the case is written down rather than left to be discovered.
